subject: MGMT363
title: Thinking Like a Business Problem Solver

questions.stem: Describe fast thinking.
options: Automatic — the answer just appears, with no effort
Effortful — you can feel yourself working through the problem step by step
Slow, deliberate, and easily interrupted by anything that demands attention
Good only at numbers and trade-offs, where the rules are already known
questions.why: Fast thinking is automatic and instant; slow thinking is effortful. See §1.1.

questions.stem: Describe slow thinking.
options: Effortful thinking you can feel yourself doing, good at new situations, numbers and trade-offs
Automatic thinking that just appears in your mind without any sense of effort, work or deliberate attention
Thinking that is always wrong because it overrides the instincts built up from experience
Thinking used only by experts, who have learned to switch off their fast reactions
questions.why: Slow thinking is effortful and tiring, but good at anything new. See §1.1.

questions.stem: Identify what fast thinking is bad at.
options: Anything it has not seen before
Familiar situations it has handled many times
Routine judgements made under time pressure
Being quick when a decision is needed at once
questions.why: Fast thinking is confident and wrong on new problems. See §1.1.

questions.stem: Explain the course in one sentence, as the chapter puts it.
options: Business problems that matter are new, and fast thinking is confident and wrong on new problems
Slow thinking should replace fast thinking everywhere, because speed is the enemy of good decisions
Problem solvers are born, not made, so the course can only help those who already have the talent
Every problem has one best answer, and the course teaches the method that finds it
questions.why: Every tool in the course forces you into slow thinking on new problems. See §1.1.

questions.stem: Identify the correct price of the ball in the bat-and-ball puzzle, and the reason most people get it wrong.
options: 5 dirhams — fast thinking answered a question it had not read properly
10 dirhams — slow thinking adds the two prices correctly to reach the total
5 dirhams — the puzzle has a trick total that most people do not notice
10 dirhams — the bat costs 100 and the ball is the remaining amount
questions.why: The ball costs 5; saying 10 is fast thinking answering too quickly. See §1.1.

questions.stem: Explain why the chapter says not to slow everything down.
options: Slow thinking is expensive; used on every decision it would paralyse you
Fast thinking is always better, because experience is more reliable than analysis
Slow thinking is only for professors, who have the time to analyse every question
Managers never have time to think, so they must learn to trust their instincts
questions.why: Most managers who 'analyse everything' are avoiding the decision. See §1.2.

questions.stem: Identify the two-question test before any decision.
options: How expensive is it to be wrong? Can I undo it?
Who is the boss on this? Who pays if it goes wrong?
Is it fast to decide? Is it cheap to implement?
Do I like the option? Does the team like it too?
questions.why: Expensive AND hard to undo → stop and use a tool from the course. See §1.2.

questions.stem: Describe a decision that should be left to fast thinking.
options: Small, reversible, and made a hundred times before
Expensive and hard to reverse, where speed matters more than care
Unfamiliar and full of numbers, where instinct is the only guide
Signing a two-year contract with a supplier the manager already knows
questions.why: Which queue to join: cost of being wrong is minutes. See §1.2.

questions.stem: Describe a decision that needs slow thinking.
options: Expensive, hard to reverse, unfamiliar, or full of numbers and trade-offs
Which supplier to phone first when two deliveries are late on the same morning
Which queue to join at the bank when both look about the same length
Who takes lunch first when two staff members both want the early break
questions.why: Hiring, pricing, signing anything: cost of being wrong is months. See §1.2.

questions.stem: Explain what makes the two-question test the most useful habit in the course.
options: It takes ten seconds and tells you which thinking mode the decision deserves
It replaces every other tool in the course once a manager has learned to use it
It makes every decision fast by removing the need to think about most of them
It removes the need for evidence, because the two questions settle the matter
questions.why: Ten seconds, before any decision. See §1.2.

questions.stem: Identify the five moves of a problem solver in order.
options: Frame, diagnose, check, generate, decide
Decide, generate, check, diagnose, frame
Plan, organise, lead, control, review
Ask, gather, analyse, decide, implement
questions.why: Frame → diagnose → check → generate → decide. See §1.3.

questions.stem: Describe the question the 'frame' move answers.
options: What exactly is the problem, and is it the right one?
What is actually causing it, and since when?
Which option is best, and why that one?
Is the evidence real, and who produced it?
questions.why: Frame asks what the problem is and whether it is the right one. See §1.3.

questions.stem: Describe the question the 'diagnose' move answers.
options: What is actually causing it?
What are my real options for fixing it?
How do I get the solution accepted?
Is this the right problem to be working on?
questions.why: Diagnose finds the cause. See §1.3.

questions.stem: Explain where most people go wrong with the five moves.
options: They hear a problem and jump straight to a solution — move four with moves one to three skipped
They spend far too long on framing the problem and never reach the diagnosis or the decision before the deadline passes
They never decide, because every option raises a new question that needs checking
They diagnose twice, once before and once after they have generated their options
questions.why: Skipping to move four is why the same problem comes back next quarter. See §1.3.

questions.stem: Explain why good problem solvers are 'slower at the start and faster at the end'.
options: They do the five moves in order, so the solution fits the real problem
They are naturally slow people who make up for it by working longer hours
They avoid decisions until the problem has become so clear that anyone could solve it
They wait for others to decide and then act quickly on what has been agreed
questions.why: Slower at the start, faster at the end. See §1.3.

questions.stem: Describe creative self-efficacy.
options: Your belief that you can produce useful new solutions
General confidence about everything you do, at work and outside it
Your IQ score and your results in school and university
Your manager's opinion of how creative you are compared with the team
questions.why: It is confidence about this particular kind of work. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Explain how creative self-efficacy affects performance.
options: Belief raises interest, which raises effort, which raises the result — and the result raises the belief
Belief has no effect on results at all, because performance depends on ability and method alone, whatever people feel
Belief lowers effort, because people who feel confident stop trying as hard
Only training affects results, and belief is simply a by-product of being trained
questions.why: The loop runs in both directions. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Explain what the sentence 'I am not creative' does.
options: It lowers effort, produces a poor result, and confirms the sentence that caused it
It protects the student from failure by lowering expectations before the work begins
It has no effect, because creativity is a fixed trait that beliefs cannot change
It improves honesty, because the student is admitting a real limitation
questions.why: The loop runs backwards too. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Explain why students are told about creative self-efficacy in week 2.
options: The belief is built by small successes on real tasks, so the course gives usable tools early
Week 2 is when the first exams start, so students need to know how confidence affects their marks from the beginning
It is the easiest topic in the course and makes a gentle start before the harder tools
It replaces the project, which students would otherwise start in week 2
questions.why: That is why the project starts in week 4 rather than week 12. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Identify the source the chapter cites for creative self-efficacy.
options: Chen, Kim, Gong and Liang (2025)
Kahneman (2011)
Doshi and Hauser (2024)
Kepner and Tregoe (1965), the KT method
questions.why: Journal of Management Studies 62(2), set reading. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Identify the three arguments that problem solving is a skill, not a personality trait.
options: It improves with training, depends on knowing the field, and depends on the method used
It is inherited from parents, fixed by early adulthood, and can be tested for reliably at birth
It needs an MBA, a management title and at least ten years of experience
It is a matter of luck, natural talent and the confidence to act on both
questions.why: Three arguments for skill, one caution. See §1.5.

questions.stem: Explain the caution the chapter adds about problem-solving skill.
options: Gains fade without practice — it is like a language, not a fact learned once
Training never works for people who do not already have the right personality
Only personality matters in the end, whatever the training programme claims
The skill cannot be measured, so nobody can say whether training has worked
questions.why: Without practice the effect decays. See §1.5.

questions.stem: Explain what finding week 5 hard tells a student, according to the chapter.
options: It is information about their practice, not about their ability
They should drop the course before the difficulty affects their other marks
They lack the personality for problem solving and should choose another career
The teacher is wrong to make week 5 so difficult for students at this stage
questions.why: The students who improve most usually do not start ahead. See §1.5.

questions.stem: Explain why knowing the field matters for problem solving.
options: You cannot diagnose a café you know nothing about — and knowledge is learnable
Only experts can think clearly about problems, so beginners should follow procedures
Knowledge replaces method, so a manager who knows the field needs no tools
Fields never change, so knowledge learned once lasts for a whole career
questions.why: Knowledge is learnable; personality is not. See §1.5.

questions.stem: Describe the evidence that problem solving improves with training.
options: Measured gains in idea fluency, problem definition and self-efficacy after structured practice
Students feel much more confident after the course and say so in the end-of-semester feedback forms
Teachers say so, based on their experience of watching students improve
Exams get easier, because students learn the kinds of question that are asked
questions.why: Measured gains after structured practice. See §1.5.

questions.stem: Describe the strength and the failure of the 'answer fast' default.
options: Decisive and people bring you problems — but you solve the wrong problem quickly
Thorough and well informed about every option — but you never decide and the chance passes you by
Good information from many sources — but you adopt the loudest view in the room
Consistent and defensible — but new problems get old answers
questions.why: Answer fast: decisive; fails by solving the wrong problem quickly. See §1.6.

questions.stem: Describe the failure of the 'gather more data' default.
options: You never decide; the chance passes
You solve the wrong problem quickly
You adopt the loudest view in the room
New problems get old answers
questions.why: Thorough, rarely embarrassed, never decides. See §1.6.

questions.stem: Describe the failure of the 'ask what others think' default.
options: You adopt the loudest view in the room
You never decide, because the group cannot agree
You solve the wrong problem, because the group frames it badly
You follow old answers, because the group prefers what it knows
questions.why: Good information, but the loudest view wins. See §1.6.

questions.stem: Describe the failure of the 'follow the procedure' default.
options: New problems get old answers
You never decide, because the procedure has too many steps
You adopt the loudest view, because the procedure is written by the most senior person
You decide too fast, because the procedure removes the need to think
questions.why: Consistent and defensible — until the problem is new. See §1.6.

questions.stem: Explain the purpose of the course regarding your default habit.
options: Not to change it, but to give you a tool for the moments when it is the wrong instrument
To replace it with a better default that works in every situation the manager will ever face at work
To remove all defaults, so that every decision is made from first principles
To make everyone answer fast, because speed is what business rewards
questions.why: Your default is largely fixed; the tool is for when it fails. See §1.6.

questions.stem: Explain why naming your own default matters.
options: It is the first step to noticing when it is about to cost you
It is graded as part of the course assessment
It changes the default into a better one over time
It impresses the client, who sees a manager who knows herself
questions.why: Naming it lets you notice it. See §1.6.

questions.stem: Identify the chapter where the 'generate' move is taught.
options: Chapters 7 and 8
Chapter 2
Chapter 3
Chapter 9 and the project
questions.why: Generate = chapters 7 and 8; decide = chapter 9. See §1.3.

questions.stem: Classify a manager who answers a new pricing question in four seconds.
options: Fast thinking on a new problem — confident and probably wrong
Slow thinking — careful analysis compressed by years of pricing experience
Expertise — an experienced manager's instant answer is almost always correct
Creative self-efficacy — the manager believes in his own ability to find the answer
questions.why: Fast thinking is wrong on new problems. See §1.1.

questions.stem: Determine the thinking mode a student used when answering '10 dirhams' to the bat-and-ball puzzle.
options: Fast thinking answering a question it had not read properly
Slow thinking with a small calculation error in the final step of the sum
Creative thinking that found an unexpected answer
Critical thinking that questioned the puzzle's assumptions
questions.why: The ball costs 5; 10 is the fast-thinking answer. See §1.1.

questions.stem: Analyse a café that keeps ordering on Tuesday because 'we always have'. Determine the thinking mode.
options: Fast thinking on a routine judgement — fine until the situation changes
Slow thinking, because the owner has weighed the options and chosen Tuesday
A skipped frame move, because nobody has asked what the problem is
Creative self-efficacy, because the owner trusts her own judgement
questions.why: 'We always order on Tuesday' is fast thinking at work. See §1.1.

questions.stem: Determine the mode the question 'Should we still order on a Tuesday?' shows.
options: Slow thinking — questioning the routine
Fast thinking — the question appears automatically
Gathering more data before deciding anything
Following the procedure that says to review orders
questions.why: Slow thinking interrupts the routine. See §1.1.

questions.stem: Classify the decision 'which staff member takes lunch first' using the two-question test.
options: Fast — cheap to get wrong and easy to undo
Slow — expensive to get wrong and hard to undo
Slow — it involves numbers and trade-offs between staff
Neither — it is a routine matter, not a decision
questions.why: Cost of being wrong: minutes. See §1.2.

questions.stem: Classify 'a two-year exclusive supplier contract for 20% off' using the two-question test.
options: Slow — expensive to get wrong and hard to undo
Fast — it saves money, so there is nothing to think about
Fast — suppliers are routine and the manager has dealt with them before
Neither — it is a discount, not a decision about the business
questions.why: Expensive AND hard to undo → stop and use a tool. See §1.2.

questions.stem: Classify 'which of two job applicants to hire'.
options: Slow — hiring is expensive and hard to reverse
Fast — people are easy to replace if the choice turns out badly
Fast — interviews are routine and the manager has run many of them
Neither — HR decides, so the manager is not making a decision at all
questions.why: Hiring: cost of being wrong is months. See §1.2.

questions.stem: Analyse 'reorder the phone case that sells out weekly'. Determine the mode and the reason.
options: Fast — made a hundred times, small and reversible
Slow — it involves money and every order affects the cash position
Slow — stock is strategic and should always be analysed carefully
Neither — the supplier decides when to deliver, not the shop
questions.why: Routine, reversible, familiar. See §1.2.

questions.stem: Analyse 'move the checkout to the other wall'. Determine which of the six decisions the chapter calls 'small but not'.
options: This one — it looks small but changes customer flow and is costly to reverse
The lunch order — it looks small but affects the whole team's afternoon
Reordering the phone case — it looks small but ties up money in stock
Replying to an angry customer — it looks small but can damage the brand online
questions.why: One looks small and is not; fast thinking would get it wrong. See Exercise 1 and §1.2.

questions.stem: Determine the right response to an angry customer at the counter.
options: Fast thinking is right — it is familiar, small and must be handled now
Slow thinking — call a meeting so that the team can agree the response
Slow thinking — gather data about the complaint before responding
Refuse to answer until the manager has had time to think about it
questions.why: Familiar situations suit fast thinking. See §1.2.

questions.stem: Analyse the Dubai clinic that sent receptionists on a 40,000-dirham course and saw no change. Determine the moves skipped.
options: Frame, diagnose and check were skipped — the meeting jumped to generate
Decide was skipped, because the manager never properly committed to the training course she bought
Generate was skipped, because only one option was ever considered
Nothing was skipped — the course was the right answer, badly delivered
questions.why: Right answer to the wrong problem: move four with one to three skipped. See Exercise 2 and §1.3.

questions.stem: Determine the thinking mode behind the manager's statement 'the receptionists are slow'.
options: Fast thinking — an instant explanation with no evidence
Slow thinking — based on the complaint data the clinic had collected
Creative mode — a new explanation nobody had thought of before
The decide move — the manager had weighed the options and chosen
questions.why: The nurse's evidence (5–7 p.m., one receptionist for three doctors) came later. See Exercise 2 and §1.1.

questions.stem: Analyse the nurse's finding that complaints came between 5 and 7 p.m. Determine the move it belongs to.
options: Diagnose — finding what is actually causing it
Frame — deciding what the problem is and whether it is the right one
Generate — producing options for fixing the problem
Decide — choosing the best option and explaining why
questions.why: Diagnose answers 'what is actually causing it?'. See §1.3.

questions.stem: Determine the move a manager performs when asking 'is this the right problem?'.
options: Frame
Diagnose
Check
Decide
questions.why: Frame = what exactly is the problem, and is it the right one. See §1.3.

questions.stem: Determine the move a manager performs when asking 'is the evidence real?'.
options: Check
Frame
Generate
Decide
questions.why: Check = is the reasoning sound and the evidence real. See §1.3.

questions.stem: Analyse why a problem solved by jumping to a solution 'comes back next quarter'. Determine the chapter's reason.
options: The cause was never diagnosed, so the fix treated the wrong thing
The solution was too cheap, so it did not go far enough
The team was lazy and did not implement the solution properly or on time
Problems always return, whatever the quality of the solution
questions.why: Skipping moves one to three is why problems return. See §1.3.

questions.stem: Analyse two students with the same mark: one says 'I am not creative', the other 'I have not learned this yet'. Determine the likely result a year later.
options: The second improves more — the belief raises effort and results
Both stay the same, because the mark reflects fixed ability
The first improves more, because honesty about weakness drives learning
Marks are fixed by personality, so neither sentence makes a difference
questions.why: Belief and performance feed each other in both directions. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Determine what a teacher should do in week 1 if belief drives performance.
options: Give small real tasks students can succeed at early, to build the belief
Give the hardest exam first so that students know how much they have to learn
Tell students that creativity is inherited so that they have realistic expectations
Delay all practice to week 12, when students have learned enough theory to succeed
questions.why: The belief is built by small successes on real tasks. See §1.4 and Exercise 3.

questions.stem: Classify the sentence 'I have not learned this yet' in terms of creative self-efficacy.
options: A belief that keeps effort up, so results can improve
A sign of low ability, because a capable student would already have learned it
A fixed personality trait that the student cannot change
An excuse for a poor mark that the student should not be allowed to use
questions.why: The loop runs forward with this sentence. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a manager who gives new staff only impossible tasks. Determine the effect on creative self-efficacy.
options: It falls — failures lower belief, which lowers effort
It rises — hard tasks build confidence by stretching people
No effect — self-efficacy is fixed by the time people start work
It depends on pay — well-paid staff can tolerate impossible tasks
questions.why: Belief is built by successes, not by failures. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Analyse the claim 'the best problem solver I know never took a course'. Determine the chapter's reply.
options: One vivid case does not disprove measured training gains; they learned by practice in their field
The claim proves that problem solving is personality, because the person had no formal training of any kind
Courses are useless, because the best problem solvers learn from experience alone
Experience never matters, because the skill comes from the method, not the field
questions.why: Skill improves with training and depends on knowing the field. See §1.5 and Exercise 3.

questions.stem: Analyse the admission that gains fade without practice. Determine whether it weakens the skill claim.
options: No — fading without practice is exactly what you expect from any skill, like a language
Yes — it proves that personality decides in the end, because real skills do not fade once they are learned
Yes — skills never fade once learned, so this must be something else
No — because the gains never fade in people who were trained properly
questions.why: A skill like a language, not a fact learned once. See §1.5.

questions.stem: Determine the chapter's explanation for a manager with an MBA who solves problems badly.
options: Skill depends on method and practice, not on a qualification
MBAs make people worse at problem solving by teaching them to rely on frameworks
Personality beats training, so the MBA was never going to make a difference
Managers never need the skill, because they have teams to solve problems for them
questions.why: It depends on the method used and on practice. See §1.5.

questions.stem: Select the evidence that best supports 'this is a skill'.
options: The same people produce better results with a structured process than without
Some people are naturally creative and others are not, whatever their training
Confident people get promoted faster than people who doubt themselves
Problem solving is a popular course that students choose when they can
questions.why: The same people, better results with method. See §1.5.

questions.stem: Classify a manager who calls a meeting for every decision and then goes with the loudest voice.
options: The 'ask what others think' default failing
The 'answer fast' default — the manager decides before the meeting starts
The 'follow the procedure' default — the meeting is required by the rules
Slow thinking — the manager is gathering views before deciding
questions.why: Good information, but you adopt the loudest view. See §1.6.

questions.stem: Classify a manager who is still collecting reports when the supplier's offer expires.
options: The 'gather more data' default — never deciding
The 'answer fast' default — deciding before the reports arrive
The 'ask others' default — waiting for the team's view
Creative self-efficacy — the manager believes more data will reveal the answer
questions.why: You never decide; the chance passes. See §1.6.

questions.stem: Classify a manager who applies last year's checklist to a brand-new problem.
options: The 'follow the procedure' default — new problems get old answers
The 'answer fast' default — the checklist gives an instant answer
The 'gather more data' default — the checklist collects information
Slow thinking — the checklist forces careful analysis
questions.why: Consistent and defensible — until the problem is new. See §1.6.

questions.stem: Analyse the clinic meeting where nobody asked the nurse. Determine the default habit most likely at work.
options: Answer fast — the manager gave an instant explanation and the meeting followed
Gather more data — the meeting wanted reports before listening to staff
Follow the procedure — the clinic's rules say that complaints go to training
Ask what others think — the meeting adopted the loudest view in the room, the manager's own
questions.why: The instant explanation stopped anyone asking the person with the evidence. See Exercise 2 and §1.6.

questions.stem: Determine the right use of knowing your default.
options: Notice the moment it is about to cost you and reach for a tool
Change your personality so that the default no longer applies
Hide it from your team so that they do not exploit it
Use it on every decision, because it is the habit you know best
questions.why: Notice when the default is the wrong instrument. See §1.6.

questions.stem: Analyse a manager who says 'I analyse everything before deciding'. Determine the chapter's warning.
options: Analysing everything is often avoiding the decision rather than improving it
That is ideal management, because every decision deserves careful thought
Fast thinking is always better, because experience beats analysis
Analysis is never useful, because the world changes before the analysis is finished
questions.why: Slow thinking applied everywhere paralyses you. See §1.2.

questions.stem: Determine why signing a contract needs slow thinking even for an experienced manager.
options: Contracts are expensive, hard to reverse and full of trade-offs — new enough to defeat fast thinking
Experience makes contracts routine, so an experienced manager can sign them quickly and safely without a second look
Fast thinking is faster, which is what matters when a supplier is waiting
Managers never sign contracts, because that is the job of the legal department
questions.why: Expensive, hard to undo, trade-offs. See §1.1 and §1.2.

questions.stem: Select the action that builds creative self-efficacy in a new team member.
options: Give them a real task they can complete and point out the success
Tell them that creativity is a gift so that they do not blame themselves for failures
Give them only observation tasks until they have learned how the team works
Criticise their first idea in public so that they learn to think more carefully
questions.why: Belief is built by small successes on real tasks. See §1.4.
